# Step 4: set up and launch your crawl

Make sure you've uploaded your data and that your files have been analyzed (they should have the status "Processed") before running your crawl!

## Set up a crawl with data ingestion.

On the crawl setup page, scroll down to the Analysis section.

Click on "Data ingestion" to expand the section.

Tick the "Enable data ingestion" box.

From the "select a file" drop-down list, choose the file you uploaded earlier. You can also choose to upload a new file at this point.

[![Image 12](https://downloads.intercomcdn.com/i/o/88425455/04e8cd08d0ae6e656a040f3a/Screenshot+2018-11-30+at+15.35.10.png?expires=1789685100&signature=19866ee8a3098e73c372dc9def5362f1cc046a6fb6335d9a1587a2a6d0a35001&req=fCgjFMx6mIQTWLcX3D%2B5hgA%2FY7KXSSqn8JyCn57USy8rzcxODD9Mvwnd%2FlHl%0AYXP914mkf8g3qYWC%0A)](https://downloads.intercomcdn.com/i/o/88425455/04e8cd08d0ae6e656a040f3a/Screenshot+2018-11-30+at+15.35.10.png?expires=1789685100&signature=19866ee8a3098e73c372dc9def5362f1cc046a6fb6335d9a1587a2a6d0a35001&req=fCgjFMx6mIQTWLcX3D%2B5hgA%2FY7KXSSqn8JyCn57USy8rzcxODD9Mvwnd%2FlHl%0AYXP914mkf8g3qYWC%0A)

**Note:**You can add multiple files.

Save your crawl setup.

## Launch the crawl with data ingestion

Launch a crawl. As URLs in the CSV file are discovered by the crawler, the information in the file is added to the information the crawler finds for that URL.

# Step 5: enjoy your enhanced crawl results

Congratulations!

You can now use the new information from your CSV file to create page segmentations.

You'll also find all of these new metrics available for filtering or adding columns to any report in the Data Explorer, or to create new segmentations. You'll find them listed "User data: [the name of your field]".

# Using CSV file format

Consistent and standards-based comma-separated values (CSV) files help make data more effective and easier to share across government.

From:[Government Digital Service](https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/government-digital-service) and [Central Digital and Data Office](https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/central-digital-and-data-office)Published:12 March 2021

Get emails about this page

## Contents

1.   Using CSV files to meet user needs
2.   When not to use CSV files
3.   Setting up your CSV file
4.   Managing large CSV files
5.   Validating your CSV files
6.   Moving or storing data in CSV file format
7.   Working with multiple database tables

Print this page

The comma-separated values (CSV) file format is widely used in government for sharing and receiving data. This guidance is for government employees who publish data. It shares the standard and best practice for creating consistent and interoperable CSV files.

The government recommends the RFC 4180 open standard for CSV files. You can read how to use this standard in the [Tabular data standard profile](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/recommended-open-standards-for-government/tabular-data-standard).

RFC 4180 aims to reduce common problems and help with data management. The standard and this guidance focus on the manual process and do not refer to using automated tools, libraries and languages. You can use some of the principles in this document in automated environments.

## Using CSV files to meet user needs

When creating a CSV file you should consider the needs of government users such as statisticians, data collection agencies, developers and data engineers.

These users need a consistent CSV file format so they can:

*   make data sets easier to share
*   aggregate data and publish it as part of the UK’s policy on open data, consistent with the principles of the [open data charter](https://opendatacharter.net/)
*   share data in the open for citizens and government workers
*   make it easier to compare data from different data sets

You should also consider whether your CSV will be read by machines or by humans, and understand how this affects the accessibility needs of your file.

The main benefits of using CSV include the ability to:

*   improve data sharing between government organisations
*   import and export CSV files to most data and analytic solutions
*   provide forward and backwards compatibility and adaptability to changing applications and requirements
*   open smaller files in a simple text editor as CSV uses a plain text format
*   improve data security - any program or malicious code in the CSV will not run when you open the file in a text editor

## When not to use CSV files

It may not be appropriate to use the CSV file format if you:

*   have large files that you query several times a day - it may be more suitable to use a different format that offers compression capabilities
*   need greater flexibility to encode additional information in the file beyond the raw data
*   need to use JSON with REST APIs - you could, however, provide a ‘Download as CSV’ option for non-technical users

It is important to note that exporting a spreadsheet to CSV format will:

*   remove any formatting such as font styles, links, borders and formulas
*   only export the current tab - single CSV does not support multiple spreadsheet tabs without reorganising your data

## Setting up your CSV file

Before you produce a CSV file, make sure the data is about one subject area. Your columns should relate to each other and not mix unrelated information. For example, you should not put employee records and budget figures in the same CSV file.

When manually setting up a CSV file, or setting up an automated process, you should:

*   include a header row to provide basic information about the file so users or machines do not need to make assumptions about column names
*   use only one header row - if you have multiple header rows, combine or merge them into a single header row
*   use one data type per column, for example do not mix numeric data and text in the same column unless you have a valid reason such as marking a value as ‘null’
*   make your column headers as simple as possible and avoid special characters, for example, ‘time period (mins)’ could become ‘time_period_mins’ or ‘time_period’
*   use commas to separate fields, especially when publishing data - do not use pipes (also known as the vertical bar symbol ‘`|`’)
*   avoid using line feed (‘\n’) and carriage return (‘\r’) characters as they can cause data import issues
*   save the file in [UTF-8](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/open-standards-for-government/cross-platform-character-encoding-profile) - this is an international standard that supports characters in most scripts and minimises errors in the import and export of files
*   use only one value per cell - do not list multiple values (arrays) in a single cell, for example “value1, value2, value3”

You should also apply metadata to your CSV files. You can learn more by reading the:

*   open standard for [CSV on the Web (CSVW)](https://w3c.github.io/csvw/)
*   guidance on [recording information about data sets you share with others](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/record-information-about-data-sets-you-share-with-others)
*   open standard for [using metadata to describe CSV data](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/recommended-open-standards-for-government/using-metadata-to-describe-csv-data)
*   [W3C guidance](https://www.w3.org/TR/tabular-data-primer/#documentation) about how to build a metadata file

## Managing large CSV files

The definition of a large CSV file will depend on the department and tool using the file. As a general guide, a CSV file size of a few hundred MB is large for Excel while a CSV file size of a few GB is large for an API or a data management tool. Keep this in mind when choosing which tools or applications to use.

When using large CSV files in Excel, you must make sure the whole file loads properly. If you are using older versions of Excel (97-2003) you should be aware that they have a low row limit of around 65,000 rows. Microsoft has information about [Excel specifications and limits](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/excel-specifications-and-limits-1672b34d-7043-467e-8e27-269d656771c3).

When CSV files become large, data suppliers might compress them into a ZIP file. If you use a ZIP file, you should [add metadata to describe your CSV](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/record-information-about-data-sets-you-share-with-others) and add instructions on how to open the ZIP file without causing errors to the contents of the file.

## Validating your CSV files

To make sure your CSV files remain accurate and consistent, you should:

*   check the data does not change when opening the file in common applications - for example, some spreadsheet tools remove leading zeros for values such as ‘0008’
*   check the application opening your CSV files recognises the column formats and their content, such as [time and date](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/open-standards-for-government/date-times-and-time-stamps-standard)
*   check the characters in the CSV columns to make sure they display correctly
*   provide guidance on any application specific problems you’re aware of
*   make sure your CSV files still open correctly if you export them from an application
*   make sure your chosen tool displays all the rows and columns

## Moving or storing data in CSV file format

When creating data sets, you should consider whether it is likely your data set will need to be transferred to or stored in different places. Using a standardised data structure makes moving data easier and helps keep it intact.

For example, the National Archives is legally required to store a range of data sets from government departments. It is easier for users to search and process these data sets if their format is standardised.

## Working with multiple database tables

You should not compress multiple database tables into one CSV file. Instead, you could use a format such as CSV on the Web to express the relationships between several separate CSV files, or use a more appropriate file format.

There may be instances where 2 tables hold very similar data, such as first name and last name. In cases like this, it might make sense to merge them into one CSV.

# Using CSV file format

Consistent and standards-based comma-separated values (CSV) files help make data more effective and easier to share across government.

From:[Government Digital Service](https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/government-digital-service) and [Central Digital and Data Office](https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/central-digital-and-data-office)Published:12 March 2021

Get emails about this page

## Contents

1.   Using CSV files to meet user needs
2.   When not to use CSV files
3.   Setting up your CSV file
4.   Managing large CSV files
5.   Validating your CSV files
6.   Moving or storing data in CSV file format
7.   Working with multiple database tables

Print this page

The comma-separated values (CSV) file format is widely used in government for sharing and receiving data. This guidance is for government employees who publish data. It shares the standard and best practice for creating consistent and interoperable CSV files.

The government recommends the RFC 4180 open standard for CSV files. You can read how to use this standard in the [Tabular data standard profile](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/recommended-open-standards-for-government/tabular-data-standard).

RFC 4180 aims to reduce common problems and help with data management. The standard and this guidance focus on the manual process and do not refer to using automated tools, libraries and languages. You can use some of the principles in this document in automated environments.

## Using CSV files to meet user needs

When creating a CSV file you should consider the needs of government users such as statisticians, data collection agencies, developers and data engineers.

These users need a consistent CSV file format so they can:

*   make data sets easier to share
*   aggregate data and publish it as part of the UK’s policy on open data, consistent with the principles of the [open data charter](https://opendatacharter.net/)
*   share data in the open for citizens and government workers
*   make it easier to compare data from different data sets

You should also consider whether your CSV will be read by machines or by humans, and understand how this affects the accessibility needs of your file.

The main benefits of using CSV include the ability to:

*   improve data sharing between government organisations
*   import and export CSV files to most data and analytic solutions
*   provide forward and backwards compatibility and adaptability to changing applications and requirements
*   open smaller files in a simple text editor as CSV uses a plain text format
*   improve data security - any program or malicious code in the CSV will not run when you open the file in a text editor

## When not to use CSV files

It may not be appropriate to use the CSV file format if you:

*   have large files that you query several times a day - it may be more suitable to use a different format that offers compression capabilities
*   need greater flexibility to encode additional information in the file beyond the raw data
*   need to use JSON with REST APIs - you could, however, provide a ‘Download as CSV’ option for non-technical users

It is important to note that exporting a spreadsheet to CSV format will:

*   remove any formatting such as font styles, links, borders and formulas
*   only export the current tab - single CSV does not support multiple spreadsheet tabs without reorganising your data

## Setting up your CSV file

Before you produce a CSV file, make sure the data is about one subject area. Your columns should relate to each other and not mix unrelated information. For example, you should not put employee records and budget figures in the same CSV file.

When manually setting up a CSV file, or setting up an automated process, you should:

*   include a header row to provide basic information about the file so users or machines do not need to make assumptions about column names
*   use only one header row - if you have multiple header rows, combine or merge them into a single header row
*   use one data type per column, for example do not mix numeric data and text in the same column unless you have a valid reason such as marking a value as ‘null’
*   make your column headers as simple as possible and avoid special characters, for example, ‘time period (mins)’ could become ‘time_period_mins’ or ‘time_period’
*   use commas to separate fields, especially when publishing data - do not use pipes (also known as the vertical bar symbol ‘`|`’)
*   avoid using line feed (‘\n’) and carriage return (‘\r’) characters as they can cause data import issues
*   save the file in [UTF-8](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/open-standards-for-government/cross-platform-character-encoding-profile) - this is an international standard that supports characters in most scripts and minimises errors in the import and export of files
*   use only one value per cell - do not list multiple values (arrays) in a single cell, for example “value1, value2, value3”

You should also apply metadata to your CSV files. You can learn more by reading the:

*   open standard for [CSV on the Web (CSVW)](https://w3c.github.io/csvw/)
*   guidance on [recording information about data sets you share with others](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/record-information-about-data-sets-you-share-with-others)
*   open standard for [using metadata to describe CSV data](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/recommended-open-standards-for-government/using-metadata-to-describe-csv-data)
*   [W3C guidance](https://www.w3.org/TR/tabular-data-primer/#documentation) about how to build a metadata file

## Managing large CSV files

The definition of a large CSV file will depend on the department and tool using the file. As a general guide, a CSV file size of a few hundred MB is large for Excel while a CSV file size of a few GB is large for an API or a data management tool. Keep this in mind when choosing which tools or applications to use.

When using large CSV files in Excel, you must make sure the whole file loads properly. If you are using older versions of Excel (97-2003) you should be aware that they have a low row limit of around 65,000 rows. Microsoft has information about [Excel specifications and limits](https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/excel-specifications-and-limits-1672b34d-7043-467e-8e27-269d656771c3).

When CSV files become large, data suppliers might compress them into a ZIP file. If you use a ZIP file, you should [add metadata to describe your CSV](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/record-information-about-data-sets-you-share-with-others) and add instructions on how to open the ZIP file without causing errors to the contents of the file.

## Validating your CSV files

To make sure your CSV files remain accurate and consistent, you should:

*   check the data does not change when opening the file in common applications - for example, some spreadsheet tools remove leading zeros for values such as ‘0008’
*   check the application opening your CSV files recognises the column formats and their content, such as [time and date](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/open-standards-for-government/date-times-and-time-stamps-standard)
*   check the characters in the CSV columns to make sure they display correctly
*   provide guidance on any application specific problems you’re aware of
*   make sure your CSV files still open correctly if you export them from an application
*   make sure your chosen tool displays all the rows and columns

## Moving or storing data in CSV file format

When creating data sets, you should consider whether it is likely your data set will need to be transferred to or stored in different places. Using a standardised data structure makes moving data easier and helps keep it intact.

For example, the National Archives is legally required to store a range of data sets from government departments. It is easier for users to search and process these data sets if their format is standardised.

## Working with multiple database tables

You should not compress multiple database tables into one CSV file. Instead, you could use a format such as CSV on the Web to express the relationships between several separate CSV files, or use a more appropriate file format.

There may be instances where 2 tables hold very similar data, such as first name and last name. In cases like this, it might make sense to merge them into one CSV.

## Introduction

A comma-separated values (CSV) file is a delimited text file that uses a comma to separate values.   

CSV file stores tabular data (numbers and text) in plain text. Each line of the file is a data record.   

Each record consists of one or more fields, separated by commas.   

The use of the comma as a field separator is the source of the name for this file format.

## Introduction

A comma-separated values (CSV) file is a delimited text file that uses a comma to separate values.   

CSV file stores tabular data (numbers and text) in plain text. Each line of the file is a data record.   

Each record consists of one or more fields, separated by commas.   

The use of the comma as a field separator is the source of the name for this file format.  
  

## How do you open them?

You can open a CSV file using MS Excel (in Windows / Mac) or using Numbers (in Mac).  
You can also create CSV files using Open Office.

## Abstract

### Question

What clinical problems prevent biomarker testing and drug therapy for non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in Japan?

### Findings

In this cohort study of 1479 patients with NSCLC, including nonadenocarcinoma, 63% to 95% of patients with _EGFR_ variation, _ALK_ fusion, _ROS1_ fusion, _BRAF_ variation, and _MET_ exon 14 skipping received targeted therapy as first-line treatment. The median overall survival of patients who were positive for driver gene alteration and received targeted therapy, did not receive targeted therapy, and were negative for driver gene alteration was 24, 15, and 11 months, respectively.

### Meaning

These findings suggest that multigene testing should be conducted for NSCLC, even in cases of nonadenocarcinoma.

## Abstract

This multicenter cohort study investigates the status of biomarker testing and drug therapy for non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in Japan to identify problems in lung cancer treatment.

## Abstract

### Importance

Biomarker testing for driver mutations is essential for selecting appropriate non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treatment but is insufficient.

### Objective

To investigate the status of biomarker testing and drug therapy for NSCLC in Japan for identifying problems in treatment.

### Design, Setting, and Participants

The REVEAL cohort study included retrospective data collection and prospective follow-up from 29 institutions across Japan. Of 1500 patients diagnosed with advanced or recurrent NSCLC between January 1 and March 18, 2021, 1479 were eligible. Cases recognized at the wrong clinical stage (n = 12), diagnosed outside the study period (n = 6), not treated according to eligibility criteria before recurrence (n = 2), and with deficient consent acquisition procedure (n = 1) were excluded.

### Main Outcomes and Measures

The primary end point was the biomarker testing status. Treatment-related factors were examined.

### Results

Among the 1479 patients included in the analysis, the median age was 72 (range, 30-95) years; 1013 (68.5%) were men; 1161 (78.5%) had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0 or 1; 1097 (74.2%) were current or past smokers; and 947 (64.0%) had adenocarcinoma. Biomarker status was confirmed in 1273 patients (86.1%). Multigene testing was performed in 705 cases (47.7%); single-gene testing, in 847 (57.3%); and both, in 279 (18.9%). Biomarker testing was performed for _EGFR_ in 1245 cases (84.2%); _ALK_, in 1165 (78.8%); _ROS1_, in 1077 (72.8%); _BRAF_, in 803 (54.3%); and _MET_, in 805 (54.4%). Positivity rates among 898 adenocarcinoma cases included 305 (34.0%) for _EGFR_, 29 (3.2%) for _ALK_, 19 (2.1%) for _ROS1_, 11 (1.2%) for _BRAF_, and 14 (1.6%) for _MET_. Positivity rates among 375 nonadenocarcinoma cases were 14 (3.7%) for _EGFR_, 6 (1.6%) for _ALK_, 1 (0.3%) for _ROS1_, 3 (0.8%) for _BRAF_, and 8 (2.1%) for _MET_. Poor physical status, squamous cell carcinoma, and other comorbidities were associated with hampered multigene testing. Targeted therapy was received as first-line treatment by 263 of 278 cases (94.6%) positive for _EGFR_, 25 of 32 (78.1%) positive for _ALK_, 15 of 24 (62.5%) positive for _ROS1_, 9 of 12 (75.0%) positive for _BRAF_, and 12 of 19 (63.2%) positive for _MET_. Median overall survival of patients with positive findings for driver gene alteration and who received targeted therapy was 24.3 (95% CI, not reported) months; with positive findings for driver gene alteration and who did not receive targeted therapy, 15.2 (95% CI, 7.7 to not reported) months; and with negative findings for driver gene alteration, 11.0 (95% CI, 10.0-12.5) months. Multigene testing for nonadenocarcinomas and adenocarcinomas accounted for 705 (47.7%) of all NSCLC cases.

### Conclusions and Relevance

These findings suggest that multigene testing has not been sufficiently implemented in Japan and should be considered prospectively, even in nonadenocarcinomas, to avoid missing rare driver gene alterations.

## Introduction

Precision medicine has become a reality. Development of targeted agents for driver gene alterations and immune checkpoint inhibitors has improved the selection of treatments for non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), based on biomarker testing results. In particular, agents targeting driver genes, such as the epidermal growth factor receptor (_EGFR_ [OMIM [131550](https://omim.org/entry/131550)]), anaplastic lymphoma kinase (_ALK_ [OMIM [105590](https://omim.org/entry/105590)]), ROS proto-oncogene 1 (_ROS1_ [OMIM [165020](https://omim.org/entry/165020)]), v-raf murine sarcoma viral oncogene homologue B1 (_BRAF_ [OMIM [164757](https://omim.org/entry/164757)]), mesenchymal–epithelial transition factor (_MET_ [OMIM [164860](https://omim.org/entry/164860)]), rearrangement during transfection (_RET_ [OMIM [164761](https://omim.org/entry/164761)]), v-Ki-ras2 Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homologue (_KRAS_ [OMIM [190070](https://omim.org/entry/190070)]), and neurotrophic tyrosine kinase receptor (_NTRK_ [OMIM [191315](https://omim.org/entry/191315), [600456](https://omim.org/entry/600456), and [191316](https://omim.org/entry/191316)]) genes, show clinically meaningful efficacy. These agents have been approved globally, including in Japan.1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8 The 2022 Guideline for Treatment of Lung Cancer of the Japan Lung Cancer Society recommends testing patients with NSCLC for multiple biomarkers, including _EGFR_ variation, _ALK_ fusion, _ROS1_ fusion, _BRAF_ variation, _MET_ exon 14 skipping, _RET_ fusion, _KRAS_ variation, _NTRK_ fusion, and programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (_PDL1_) expression.9

Owing to the increasing number of genes binding with high affinity to a drug (ie, druggable), biomarker testing methods have shifted from single-gene methods such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), immunohistochemistry (IHC), and fluorescence in situ hybridization to multigene methods such as next-generation sequencing (NGS). In Japan, the transition to multigene testing has accelerated with the approval of an NGS-based multigene panel targeting 46 genes (the Oncomine Dx Target Test [DxTT] multiple companion diagnostic test [CDx] system; Thermo Fisher Scientific) in 2019 and a PCR test to evaluate simultaneously the presence of 11 driver genes in lung cancer (AmoyDx Pan Lung Cancer PCR Panel; Riken Genesis) in 2020. The Oncomine DxTT multiple CDx system is an NGS panel for NSCLC testing that uses high-throughput, parallel sequencing to detect sequence variations in 46 genes in DNA and RNA isolated from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded specimens or fresh frozen tumor samples. The Lung Cancer Compact Panel diagnostic multiplex CDx system (DNA Chip Research Inc), using NGS technology, was approved in 2022. Three multigene tests have been used to determine the initial treatment of patients with NSCLC in Japan. The OncoGuide NCC Oncopanel system (Sysmex Corporation), FoundationOne CDx cancer genomic profile (Foundation Medicine), and FoundationOne Liquid CDx cancer genomic profile (Foundation Medicine) are used as comprehensive genomic profiling tests. However, these tests require patients to complete the standard of care and cannot be used for the initial treatment selection of NSCLC. Following the approval of these testing methods, multigene testing has gradually spread in Japan. The clinical characteristics of patients who underwent multigene testing at a limited number of institutions have been reviewed.10 However, some patients with advanced or recurrent NSCLC have not been sufficiently investigated for driver genes prior to their initial treatment. Furthermore, information regarding the backgrounds of cases in which biomarker testing was not performed is insufficient. Therefore, we designed a multicenter, retrospective, and partially prospective study (West Japan Oncology Group [WJOG] 15421L) to investigate the actual status of biomarker testing and drug therapy for NSCLC in Japan to identify problems in lung cancer treatment.

## Methods

### Eligibility

In the REVEAL cohort study, patients histologically or cytologically diagnosed with advanced or recurrent NSCLC between July 1, 2020, and June 30, 2021, were eligible. The study was conducted in compliance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki11 and was approved by the central review board of the Tottori University Faculty of Medicine. The patients provided written informed consent. The study was registered in the University Hospital Medical Information Network Center.12 We followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology ([STROBE](https://www.equator-network.org/reporting-guidelines/strobe/)) reporting guideline.

### Study Design

The REVEAL study is a multicenter retrospective data collection and prospective follow-up study that recruited patients from 29 institutions affiliated with the WJOG in Japan. Data were collected from clinical records. The primary end point was the actual status of biomarker testing. The following issues were investigated: the proportion of genetic biomarker tests performed, the testing rate of each biomarker, success rate of biomarker tests, positivity rate for each biomarker, percentage of patients who received the relevant targeted therapy based on the results of each biomarker test, and background factors associated with the lack of multigene testing.

The clinical information related to several parameters was obtained. These included patients’ clinical background, sample collection methods, sites undergoing biopsy for diagnosis and biomarker testing, biomarker testing methods and results, details of drug therapy (range, 1-3 regimens), and efficacy.

### Statistical Analysis

Patient backgrounds were analyzed. The positivity rate for each driver gene was defined as the number of patients with positive findings divided by the number of tests performed. The number of tests performed was considered irrespective of whether the test was successful or not. Summary statistics were calculated for the patients’ backgrounds and were summarized descriptively. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses and a backward stepwise regression procedure were used to evaluate the clinical backgrounds associated with multigene testing. The cumulative survival rates were calculated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and the comparison between the subgroups was evaluated using a log-rank test. We used SAS, version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc), and pandas, version 1.5.3, NumPy, version 1.24.2, SciPy version 1.10.0, statsmodels, version 0.13.5, and lifelines, version 0.27.4 (Python Data Analysis Library) for statistical analysis. Two-sided _P_< .05 indicated statistical significance.

## Results

### Patient Characteristics

Among the 1500 patients enrolled between January 1 and March 18, 2021, 21 were excluded from the analysis. Twelve cases were recognized at the wrong clinical stage, 6 were diagnosed outside the defined period for this study, 2 were not treated according to eligibility criteria before recurrence, and for 1, the consent acquisition procedure was deficient. The baseline characteristics of the 1479 patients included in the analysis are summarized in Table 1. The median patient age was 72 (range, 30-95) years; 1013 (68.5%) were men and 466 (31.5%) were women. A total of 1161 patients (78.5%) had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG-PS) score of 0 or 1, whereas 130 (8.8%) had an ECOG-PS score of 3 or 4. A total of 947 patients (64.0%) had adenocarcinoma and 344 (23.3%) had squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Nonadenocarcinoma–non-SCC NSCLC, including NSCLC not otherwise specified, large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, and all others not diagnosed as adenocarcinoma or SCC totaled 177 (12.0%). Among the 1479 patients included in the analysis, 1192 (80.6%) had advanced-stage cancer, 57 (3.8%) experienced recurrence after chemoradiotherapy, and 230 (15.6%) experienced postoperative recurrence.

### Sampling Method and Biopsy Site

The sampling methods and biopsy sites are summarized in eTable 1 in Supplement 1. Bronchoscopy was performed in 864 patients (58.4%). Transbronchial biopsy, with or without endobronchial ultrasonography with a guide sheath, was the most common procedure, conducted in 703 patients (47.5%). A total of 970 patients (65.6%) underwent biopsy from the primary tumor and 185 (12.5%) from the metastatic lymph nodes.

### Proportion of Genetic Biomarker Tests

The proportions of genetic biomarker tests performed are summarized in Figure 1. A total of 1273 patients (86.1%) had a confirmed biomarker status. Multigene testing was performed in 705 cases (47.7%) and single-gene testing in 847 (57.3%). Both multigene and single-gene tests were performed in 279 cases (18.9%). However, genetic biomarker testing was not performed in 206 patients (13.9%). Multigene testing was performed in 485 cases with adenocarcinoma (51.3%) and 218 with nonadenocarcinoma (41.2%). Oncomine DxTT was used for multigene testing in 474 cases (67.2%). Biomarker testing was performed for _EGFR_ in 1245 cases (84.2%); _ALK_, in 1165 (78.8%); _ROS1_, in 1077 (72.8%); _BRAF_, in 803 (54.3%); and _MET_, in 805 (54.4%) (Figure 2).

### Success Rate of Genetic Biomarker Tests

The success rates of each test are summarized in eTable 2 in Supplement 1. DNA and RNA analysis of Oncomine DxTT succeeded in 449 (94.7%) and 431 (90.9%) of the 474 cases with performed tests, respectively. Single-gene tests for _EGFR_ showed 98.9% accuracy; for _ALK_, 99.1%; for _ROS1_, 91.9%; for _BRAF,_ 93.9%; and for _MET_, 99.0%. The success rates of single-gene and multigene tests by sampling method are shown in eTable 3 in Supplement 1.

### Positivity Rate for Each Driver Gene

The positivity rates for each driver gene are shown in the eFigure in Supplement 1. In all 898 adenocarcinoma cases, positivity for the _EGFR_ variation occurred in 305 (34.0%); for _ALK_ fusion, 29 (3.2%); for _ROS1_ fusion, 19 (2.1%); for the _BRAF_ V600E variation, 11 (1.2%); and for _MET_ exon 14 skipping, 14 (1.6%) (eFigure in Supplement 1). In all 375 nonadenocarcinoma cases, the positivity for the _EGFR_ variation occurred in 14 (3.7%); for _ALK_ fusion, 6 (1.6%); for _ROS1_ fusion, 1 (0.3%); for the _BRAF_ V600E mutation, 3 (0.8%); and for _MET_ exon 14 skipping, 8 (2.1%) (eFigure in Supplement 1).

### Concordance Rate of Biomarker Tests

eTable 4 in Supplement 1 summarizes the concordance of the test results for cases in which multigene and single-gene testing were performed. The positive concordance rate for multigene testing was 58 of 62 (93.5%) for _EGFR_, 4 of 6 (66.7%) for _ALK_, 3 of 5 (60.0%) for _ROS1_, 1 of 1 (100%) for _BRAF,_ and 10 of 10 (100%) for _MET_ when the single-gene testing result was a true positive. The negative concordance rates were 140 of 142 (98.6%) for _EGFR_, 160 of 160 (100%) for _ALK_, 115 of 116 (99.1%) for _ROS1_, 19 of 19 (100%) for _BRAF_, and 15 of 18 (83.3%) for _MET_.

For _EGFR_ and _ALK_, all 8 patients with negative multigene test results and positive single-gene test results received targeted therapy, with a response in 7 of 8 (87.5%). However, for _ROS1_ and _MET_, none of the patients with negative multigene test results and positive single-gene test results received targeted therapy at the clinician’s discretion (0 of 6).

### Background Factors Associated With the Lack of Multigene Testing

Univariate and multivariate analyses were performed to reveal trends in cases where multigene testing was not performed (Table 2). In univariate analysis, cases with ECOG-PS 3 or 4 (odds ratio [OR], 0.47 [95% CI, 0.32-0.70]; _P_< .001) and ECOG-PS 2 (OR, 0.74 [95% CI, 0.54-1.01]; _P_ = .06) were less likely to undergo multigene testing than were those with ECOG-PS 0 or 1; those with comorbidities were significantly less likely than those with no comorbidities to undergo multigene testing (OR, 0.50 [95% CI, 0.41-0.62]; _P_< .005). However, patients with adenocarcinoma were significantly more likely to undergo multigene testing than those with nonadenocarcinoma (OR, 0.66 [95% CI, 0.5-0.82]; _P_< .005). In the multivariate model, 3 factors, namely, ECOG-PS 3 or 4 (OR, 0.47 [95% CI, 0.32-0.70]; _P_< .005), comorbidities (OR, 0.54 [95% CI, 0.44-0.67]; _P_< .005), and nonadenocarcinoma (OR, 0.70 [95% CI, 0.56-0.87]; _P_< .005), remained associated with negative multigene test results.

### Treatment and Survival Outcome

Of the 1467 patients for whom treatment information was available, 1174 (80.0%) received any systemic therapy and 293 (20.0%) received only the best supportive care (eTable 5 in Supplement 1). At the time of data cutoff in March 2022 (median follow-up of 10.3 [range, 0-24.3] months), 719 patients (61.2%) had received 1 regimen, 253 (21.6%) had received 2 regimens, and 202 (17.2%) had received 3 or more regimens. Of the 357 patients harboring druggable driver alterations, 324 (90.8%) had received targeted therapy.

Details of the first-line treatments received by patients with positive results for each driver gene change are shown in eTable 6 in Supplement 1. The proportion of patients who received targeted therapy as first line were 263 of 278 (94.6%) with _EGFR_ variations, 25 of 32 (78.1%) with _ALK_ fusion, 15 of 24 (62.5%) with _ROS1_ fusion, 9 of 12 (75.0%) with the _BRAF_ V600E variation, and 12 of 19 (63.2%) with _MET_ exon 14 skipping. eTable 7 in Supplement 1 shows the patient background of both the groups, the one that received targeted therapy and the one that did not. We observed a trend of more women having received targeted therapy. Nonadenocarcinomas were more common in the group that did not receive targeted therapy. The median overall survival of patients with positive results for the driver gene alteration who received targeted therapy was 24.3 (95% CI, not reported) months; for those with positive findings for the driver gene alteration who did not receive targeted therapy, 15.2 (95% CI, 7.7 to not reported); and for those with negative findings for the driver gene alteration, 11.0 (95% CI, 10.0-12.5) months (_P_< .001) (Figure 3).

## Discussion

To our knowledge, no reports have shown the current status of biomarker testing independently of histological subtype and patient background in Japan. This study revealed the real-world status of biomarker testing in patients with unresectable, advanced, or recurrent NSCLC. Multigene testing in Japan is not sufficiently implemented for nonadenocarcinomas and adenocarcinomas, accounting for 705 (47.7%) of all NSCLC cases.

Use of multigene testing has increased in the US, from 28.3% in 2015 to 68.1% in 2020.13 Contrastingly, in many Asian countries, such as China, Malaysia, and Thailand, multigene testing has not been introduced, and genetic tests other than those for _EGFR_ and _ALK_ are not reimbursed.14,15,16 Asian lung cancer experts have provided consensus recommendations for NSCLC biomarker testing for clinicians working in Asia to improve patient care. These guidelines state that along with programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (_PDL1_) expression, clinicians should assess for driver alterations in _EGFR_, _ALK_, and _ROS1_ simultaneously, as biomarker testing before initial therapy of metastatic adenocarcinoma and depending on the resources and therapeutic products available, potentially informative or actionable alterations should also be assessed in other genes (_BRAF_ V600E, _RET_, _MET_ exon 14 skipping, _KRAS_, _ERBB2_, and _NTRK_).17

Furthermore, if multiple genes are tested, a panel test should be considered rather than sequential single-gene testing for individual biomarkers. In Japan, several points have been reached through expert consensus. The REVEAL study data showed high _EGFR_, _ALK_, and _ROS1_ testing rates. Tests for other druggable genes, such as _BRAF_ and _RET_, are available. However, approximately half of the cases in the REVEAL study did not undergo multigene testing. This is a key issue in the treatment of lung cancer in Japan. It is necessary that Japan, along with other Asian countries, should promote multigene testing as a common goal.

The proportion of multigene testing was directly reflected in the _BRAF_ and _MET_ testing rates. In Japan, NGS-based tests are used as CDx for targeted agents in _BRAF_ and _MET_ alteration-positive NSCLC. Multigene testing has become increasingly important because some drivers, such as the _RET_ fusion, have recently been approved only for multigene testing as a CDx for targeted therapy. More widely implemented multigene testing is essential for administering targeted therapies to patients with rare genetic drivers. However, the success rate after the initial introduction of the Oncomine DxTT multiple CDx system was insufficient in a recent study.10 Therefore, the quantity and quality of the specimens require optimization. These results possibly occurred because the higher specimen quality and quantity required for this test was compared with that needed for single-gene testing. This is one of the most substantial factors contributing to the lack of widespread use of multigene testing in Japan. It is generally recognized that surgical specimens, for which more specimens are available, are more suitable for genetic testing; however, this was not the case with the REVEAL study. Therefore, further detailed investigations are warranted. The efforts of clinicians to improve the quantity and quality of biopsy specimens have improved success rates. The 2 approved multigene tests that allow for variations in the required quality and quantity of specimens would further benefit clinicians by allowing them to use specimens with varying quality and quantity, depending on the condition of the specimen.

The results of multigene tests can differ from those of single-gene tests, as in the discordant cases in this study. There are 2 main reasons for this finding. First, due to the characteristics of NGS, it tends to be less sensitive than PCR and other tests. Second, the coverage of each test differs for each genetic alteration subtype. In the REVEAL study data, although a small number of cases was analyzed, a trend toward lower positive concordance rates for _ALK_ and _ROS1_ and lower negative concordance rates for _MET_ occurred, because false-positive findings for _MET_ exon 14 skipping have been reported with the Oncomine DxTT, which is not approved as a CDx, and validation with single-gene testing is recommended.18

Similarly, IHC, as single-gene testing for _ROS1,_ has not been approved as a CDx due to the high number of false-positive findings reported (eTable 8 in Supplement 1).19 However, IHC, as single-gene testing for _ALK,_ which has high sensitivity, has been approved as a CDx (eTable 8 in Supplement 1). The quality and quantity of specimens submitted to Oncomine DxTT may have affected the results; however, this is unknown, because such information was not collected in the REVEAL study.

Poor ECOG-PS, SCC, and other comorbidities were background factors associated with not performing multigene testing. _MET_ alterations are frequently detected in nonadenocarcinoma,20 similar to our data. There is concern that _MET_ alterations might be frequently missed by single-gene testing because they are less frequent and tend to be a lower priority for testing. Therefore, multigene testing should be performed more frequently in patients without adenocarcinoma. In addition, some targeted therapies, such as osimertinib mesylate21,22 and alectinib hydrochloride,23 have been safely administered to patients with poor ECOG-PS. In vulnerable patients, treatment options are limited. Therefore, providing opportunities for these patients to undergo multigene testing is important. Furthermore, perioperative treatments for NSCLC positive for driver gene alterations have been developed, and further discussion is needed on when and which genes should be tested.

Approximately 90% of patients harboring any druggable driver alteration in this study received at least 1 targeted therapy. However, when considering each driver gene, driver alterations other than those in _EGFR_ were found to have lower rates of targeted induction as a first-line therapy. Shimizu et al24 showed that first-line treatment with an EGFR–tyrosine kinase inhibitor in the single-gene testing era was administered to 93.3% of patients with positive test results for the biomarker; _ALK_ inhibitor, to 93.3%; and ROS1 inhibitor, to 100%. The discrepancy between the previous report and the REVEAL study results can be attributed to the fact that the study did not strictly assess the status of biomarker testing before the initial treatment and that the results of biomarker testing were only known in some cases after the first-line treatment had been initiated. The prognosis for patients with positive findings for the driver gene alteration without targeted therapy was not different from that for patients with negative findings in the REVEAL study.25 In addition, some patients with positive findings for the driver gene alteration did not receive target therapy. There could be background difficulties in providing targeted therapies; however, we hope that appropriate therapies are provided as much as possible. The prognosis of patients with advanced or recurrent lung cancer could be improved by performing appropriate biomarker testing and initiating the relevant targeted therapies.

### Limitations

This study has several limitations. The data set is not a collection of consecutive cases; therefore, selection bias cannot be eliminated. However, this bias could be minimized by entering a large number of cases (eg, 1500) from numerous facilities. In addition, as stated previously, certain results of biomarker testing were only known after the initiation of first-line treatment. Finally, the study has limited generalizability to a broader population because the investigational sites were institutions that joined the WJOG and requested participation. Most were specialized cancer care institutions. These results may not reflect the approaches to biomarker testing in institutions without specialists.

## Conclusions

The findings of the REVEAL cohort study suggest that multigene testing has not been sufficiently implemented in Japan and should be performed even in nonadenocarcinomas and patients with poor ECOG-PS to avoid missing rare driver gene alterations. Follow-up data, including mature data on treatment and survival, will be analyzed in the REVEAL trial in the future.

## Abstract

### Question

What clinical problems prevent biomarker testing and drug therapy for non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in Japan?

### Findings

In this cohort study of 1479 patients with NSCLC, including nonadenocarcinoma, 63% to 95% of patients with _EGFR_ variation, _ALK_ fusion, _ROS1_ fusion, _BRAF_ variation, and _MET_ exon 14 skipping received targeted therapy as first-line treatment. The median overall survival of patients who were positive for driver gene alteration and received targeted therapy, did not receive targeted therapy, and were negative for driver gene alteration was 24, 15, and 11 months, respectively.

### Meaning

These findings suggest that multigene testing should be conducted for NSCLC, even in cases of nonadenocarcinoma.

## Abstract

This multicenter cohort study investigates the status of biomarker testing and drug therapy for non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in Japan to identify problems in lung cancer treatment.

## Abstract

### Importance

Biomarker testing for driver mutations is essential for selecting appropriate non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treatment but is insufficient.

### Objective

To investigate the status of biomarker testing and drug therapy for NSCLC in Japan for identifying problems in treatment.

### Design, Setting, and Participants

The REVEAL cohort study included retrospective data collection and prospective follow-up from 29 institutions across Japan. Of 1500 patients diagnosed with advanced or recurrent NSCLC between January 1 and March 18, 2021, 1479 were eligible. Cases recognized at the wrong clinical stage (n = 12), diagnosed outside the study period (n = 6), not treated according to eligibility criteria before recurrence (n = 2), and with deficient consent acquisition procedure (n = 1) were excluded.

### Main Outcomes and Measures

The primary end point was the biomarker testing status. Treatment-related factors were examined.

### Results

Among the 1479 patients included in the analysis, the median age was 72 (range, 30-95) years; 1013 (68.5%) were men; 1161 (78.5%) had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0 or 1; 1097 (74.2%) were current or past smokers; and 947 (64.0%) had adenocarcinoma. Biomarker status was confirmed in 1273 patients (86.1%). Multigene testing was performed in 705 cases (47.7%); single-gene testing, in 847 (57.3%); and both, in 279 (18.9%). Biomarker testing was performed for _EGFR_ in 1245 cases (84.2%); _ALK_, in 1165 (78.8%); _ROS1_, in 1077 (72.8%); _BRAF_, in 803 (54.3%); and _MET_, in 805 (54.4%). Positivity rates among 898 adenocarcinoma cases included 305 (34.0%) for _EGFR_, 29 (3.2%) for _ALK_, 19 (2.1%) for _ROS1_, 11 (1.2%) for _BRAF_, and 14 (1.6%) for _MET_. Positivity rates among 375 nonadenocarcinoma cases were 14 (3.7%) for _EGFR_, 6 (1.6%) for _ALK_, 1 (0.3%) for _ROS1_, 3 (0.8%) for _BRAF_, and 8 (2.1%) for _MET_. Poor physical status, squamous cell carcinoma, and other comorbidities were associated with hampered multigene testing. Targeted therapy was received as first-line treatment by 263 of 278 cases (94.6%) positive for _EGFR_, 25 of 32 (78.1%) positive for _ALK_, 15 of 24 (62.5%) positive for _ROS1_, 9 of 12 (75.0%) positive for _BRAF_, and 12 of 19 (63.2%) positive for _MET_. Median overall survival of patients with positive findings for driver gene alteration and who received targeted therapy was 24.3 (95% CI, not reported) months; with positive findings for driver gene alteration and who did not receive targeted therapy, 15.2 (95% CI, 7.7 to not reported) months; and with negative findings for driver gene alteration, 11.0 (95% CI, 10.0-12.5) months. Multigene testing for nonadenocarcinomas and adenocarcinomas accounted for 705 (47.7%) of all NSCLC cases.

### Conclusions and Relevance

These findings suggest that multigene testing has not been sufficiently implemented in Japan and should be considered prospectively, even in nonadenocarcinomas, to avoid missing rare driver gene alterations.

## Introduction

Precision medicine has become a reality. Development of targeted agents for driver gene alterations and immune checkpoint inhibitors has improved the selection of treatments for non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), based on biomarker testing results. In particular, agents targeting driver genes, such as the epidermal growth factor receptor (_EGFR_ [OMIM [131550](https://omim.org/entry/131550)]), anaplastic lymphoma kinase (_ALK_ [OMIM [105590](https://omim.org/entry/105590)]), ROS proto-oncogene 1 (_ROS1_ [OMIM [165020](https://omim.org/entry/165020)]), v-raf murine sarcoma viral oncogene homologue B1 (_BRAF_ [OMIM [164757](https://omim.org/entry/164757)]), mesenchymal–epithelial transition factor (_MET_ [OMIM [164860](https://omim.org/entry/164860)]), rearrangement during transfection (_RET_ [OMIM [164761](https://omim.org/entry/164761)]), v-Ki-ras2 Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homologue (_KRAS_ [OMIM [190070](https://omim.org/entry/190070)]), and neurotrophic tyrosine kinase receptor (_NTRK_ [OMIM [191315](https://omim.org/entry/191315), [600456](https://omim.org/entry/600456), and [191316](https://omim.org/entry/191316)]) genes, show clinically meaningful efficacy. These agents have been approved globally, including in Japan.1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8 The 2022 Guideline for Treatment of Lung Cancer of the Japan Lung Cancer Society recommends testing patients with NSCLC for multiple biomarkers, including _EGFR_ variation, _ALK_ fusion, _ROS1_ fusion, _BRAF_ variation, _MET_ exon 14 skipping, _RET_ fusion, _KRAS_ variation, _NTRK_ fusion, and programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (_PDL1_) expression.9

Owing to the increasing number of genes binding with high affinity to a drug (ie, druggable), biomarker testing methods have shifted from single-gene methods such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), immunohistochemistry (IHC), and fluorescence in situ hybridization to multigene methods such as next-generation sequencing (NGS). In Japan, the transition to multigene testing has accelerated with the approval of an NGS-based multigene panel targeting 46 genes (the Oncomine Dx Target Test [DxTT] multiple companion diagnostic test [CDx] system; Thermo Fisher Scientific) in 2019 and a PCR test to evaluate simultaneously the presence of 11 driver genes in lung cancer (AmoyDx Pan Lung Cancer PCR Panel; Riken Genesis) in 2020. The Oncomine DxTT multiple CDx system is an NGS panel for NSCLC testing that uses high-throughput, parallel sequencing to detect sequence variations in 46 genes in DNA and RNA isolated from formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded specimens or fresh frozen tumor samples. The Lung Cancer Compact Panel diagnostic multiplex CDx system (DNA Chip Research Inc), using NGS technology, was approved in 2022. Three multigene tests have been used to determine the initial treatment of patients with NSCLC in Japan. The OncoGuide NCC Oncopanel system (Sysmex Corporation), FoundationOne CDx cancer genomic profile (Foundation Medicine), and FoundationOne Liquid CDx cancer genomic profile (Foundation Medicine) are used as comprehensive genomic profiling tests. However, these tests require patients to complete the standard of care and cannot be used for the initial treatment selection of NSCLC. Following the approval of these testing methods, multigene testing has gradually spread in Japan. The clinical characteristics of patients who underwent multigene testing at a limited number of institutions have been reviewed.10 However, some patients with advanced or recurrent NSCLC have not been sufficiently investigated for driver genes prior to their initial treatment. Furthermore, information regarding the backgrounds of cases in which biomarker testing was not performed is insufficient. Therefore, we designed a multicenter, retrospective, and partially prospective study (West Japan Oncology Group [WJOG] 15421L) to investigate the actual status of biomarker testing and drug therapy for NSCLC in Japan to identify problems in lung cancer treatment.

## Methods

### Eligibility

In the REVEAL cohort study, patients histologically or cytologically diagnosed with advanced or recurrent NSCLC between July 1, 2020, and June 30, 2021, were eligible. The study was conducted in compliance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki11 and was approved by the central review board of the Tottori University Faculty of Medicine. The patients provided written informed consent. The study was registered in the University Hospital Medical Information Network Center.12 We followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology ([STROBE](https://www.equator-network.org/reporting-guidelines/strobe/)) reporting guideline.

### Study Design

The REVEAL study is a multicenter retrospective data collection and prospective follow-up study that recruited patients from 29 institutions affiliated with the WJOG in Japan. Data were collected from clinical records. The primary end point was the actual status of biomarker testing. The following issues were investigated: the proportion of genetic biomarker tests performed, the testing rate of each biomarker, success rate of biomarker tests, positivity rate for each biomarker, percentage of patients who received the relevant targeted therapy based on the results of each biomarker test, and background factors associated with the lack of multigene testing.

The clinical information related to several parameters was obtained. These included patients’ clinical background, sample collection methods, sites undergoing biopsy for diagnosis and biomarker testing, biomarker testing methods and results, details of drug therapy (range, 1-3 regimens), and efficacy.

### Statistical Analysis

Patient backgrounds were analyzed. The positivity rate for each driver gene was defined as the number of patients with positive findings divided by the number of tests performed. The number of tests performed was considered irrespective of whether the test was successful or not. Summary statistics were calculated for the patients’ backgrounds and were summarized descriptively. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses and a backward stepwise regression procedure were used to evaluate the clinical backgrounds associated with multigene testing. The cumulative survival rates were calculated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and the comparison between the subgroups was evaluated using a log-rank test. We used SAS, version 9.4 (SAS Institute Inc), and pandas, version 1.5.3, NumPy, version 1.24.2, SciPy version 1.10.0, statsmodels, version 0.13.5, and lifelines, version 0.27.4 (Python Data Analysis Library) for statistical analysis. Two-sided _P_< .05 indicated statistical significance.

## Results

### Patient Characteristics

Among the 1500 patients enrolled between January 1 and March 18, 2021, 21 were excluded from the analysis. Twelve cases were recognized at the wrong clinical stage, 6 were diagnosed outside the defined period for this study, 2 were not treated according to eligibility criteria before recurrence, and for 1, the consent acquisition procedure was deficient. The baseline characteristics of the 1479 patients included in the analysis are summarized in Table 1. The median patient age was 72 (range, 30-95) years; 1013 (68.5%) were men and 466 (31.5%) were women. A total of 1161 patients (78.5%) had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG-PS) score of 0 or 1, whereas 130 (8.8%) had an ECOG-PS score of 3 or 4. A total of 947 patients (64.0%) had adenocarcinoma and 344 (23.3%) had squamous cell carcinoma (SCC). Nonadenocarcinoma–non-SCC NSCLC, including NSCLC not otherwise specified, large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, and all others not diagnosed as adenocarcinoma or SCC totaled 177 (12.0%). Among the 1479 patients included in the analysis, 1192 (80.6%) had advanced-stage cancer, 57 (3.8%) experienced recurrence after chemoradiotherapy, and 230 (15.6%) experienced postoperative recurrence.

### Sampling Method and Biopsy Site

The sampling methods and biopsy sites are summarized in eTable 1 in Supplement 1. Bronchoscopy was performed in 864 patients (58.4%). Transbronchial biopsy, with or without endobronchial ultrasonography with a guide sheath, was the most common procedure, conducted in 703 patients (47.5%). Endobronchial ultrasonography–guided transbronchial needle aspiration was performed in 148 patients (10.0%) and bronchial lavage in 13 (0.9%). Other than bronchoscopy, testing was performed on samples obtained by transcutaneous needle biopsy in 152 cases (10.3%), surgical resection in 122 (8.2%), and pleural effusion in 113 (7.6%). A total of 970 patients (65.6%) underwent biopsy from the primary tumor and 185 (12.5%) from the metastatic lymph nodes.

### Proportion of Genetic Biomarker Tests

The proportions of genetic biomarker tests performed are summarized in Figure 1. A total of 1273 patients (86.1%) had a confirmed biomarker status. Multigene testing was performed in 705 cases (47.7%) and single-gene testing in 847 (57.3%). Both multigene and single-gene tests were performed in 279 cases (18.9%). However, genetic biomarker testing was not performed in 206 patients (13.9%). Multigene testing was performed in 485 cases with adenocarcinoma (51.3%) and 218 with nonadenocarcinoma (41.2%). Oncomine DxTT was used for multigene testing in 474 cases (67.2%). Biomarker testing was performed for _EGFR_ in 1245 cases (84.2%); _ALK_, in 1165 (78.8%); _ROS1_, in 1077 (72.8%); _BRAF_, in 803 (54.3%); and _MET_, in 805 (54.4%) (Figure 2).

### Success Rate of Genetic Biomarker Tests

The success rates of each test are summarized in eTable 2 in Supplement 1. DNA and RNA analysis of Oncomine DxTT succeeded in 449 (94.7%) and 431 (90.9%) of the 474 cases with performed tests, respectively. Single-gene tests for _EGFR_ showed 98.9% accuracy; for _ALK_, 99.1%; for _ROS1_, 91.9%; for _BRAF,_ 93.9%; and for _MET_, 99.0%. The success rates of single-gene and multigene tests by sampling method are shown in eTable 3 in Supplement 1.

### Positivity Rate for Each Driver Gene

The positivity rates for each driver gene are shown in the eFigure in Supplement 1. In all 898 adenocarcinoma cases, positivity for the _EGFR_ variation occurred in 305 (34.0%); for _ALK_ fusion, 29 (3.2%); for _ROS1_ fusion, 19 (2.1%); for the _BRAF_ V600E variation, 11 (1.2%); and for _MET_ exon 14 skipping, 14 (1.6%) (eFigure in Supplement 1). In all 375 nonadenocarcinoma cases, the positivity for the _EGFR_ variation occurred in 14 (3.7%); for _ALK_ fusion, 6 (1.6%); for _ROS1_ fusion, 1 (0.3%); for the _BRAF_ V600E mutation, 3 (0.8%); and for _MET_ exon 14 skipping, 8 (2.1%) (eFigure in Supplement 1).

### Concordance Rate of Biomarker Tests

eTable 4 in Supplement 1 summarizes the concordance of the test results for cases in which multigene and single-gene testing were performed. The positive concordance rate for multigene testing was 58 of 62 (93.5%) for _EGFR_, 4 of 6 (66.7%) for _ALK_, 3 of 5 (60.0%) for _ROS1_, 1 of 1 (100%) for _BRAF,_ and 10 of 10 (100%) for _MET_ when the single-gene testing result was a true positive. The negative concordance rates were 140 of 142 (98.6%) for _EGFR_, 160 of 160 (100%) for _ALK_, 115 of 116 (99.1%) for _ROS1_, 19 of 19 (100%) for _BRAF_, and 15 of 18 (83.3%) for _MET_.

For _EGFR_ and _ALK_, all 8 patients with negative multigene test results and positive single-gene test results received targeted therapy, with a response in 7 of 8 (87.5%). However, for _ROS1_ and _MET_, none of the patients with negative multigene test results and positive single-gene test results received targeted therapy at the clinician’s discretion (0 of 6).

### Background Factors Associated With the Lack of Multigene Testing

Univariate and multivariate analyses were performed to reveal trends in cases where multigene testing was not performed (Table 2). In univariate analysis, cases with ECOG-PS 3 or 4 (odds ratio [OR], 0.47 [95% CI, 0.32-0.70]; _P_< .001) and ECOG-PS 2 (OR, 0.74 [95% CI, 0.54-1.01]; _P_ = .06) were less likely to undergo multigene testing than were those with ECOG-PS 0 or 1; those with comorbidities were significantly less likely than those with no comorbidities to undergo multigene testing (OR, 0.50 [95% CI, 0.41-0.62]; _P_< .005). However, patients with adenocarcinoma were significantly more likely to undergo multigene testing than those with nonadenocarcinoma (OR, 0.66 [95% CI, 0.5-0.82]; _P_< .005). In the multivariate model, 3 factors, namely, ECOG-PS 3 or 4 (OR, 0.47 [95% CI, 0.32-0.70]; _P_< .005), comorbidities (OR, 0.54 [95% CI, 0.44-0.67]; _P_< .005), and nonadenocarcinoma (OR, 0.70 [95% CI, 0.56-0.87]; _P_< .005), remained associated with negative multigene test results.

### Treatment and Survival Outcome

Of the 1467 patients for whom treatment information was available, 1174 (80.0%) received any systemic therapy and 293 (20.0%) received only the best supportive care (eTable 5 in Supplement 1). At the time of data cutoff in March 2022 (median follow-up of 10.3 [range, 0-24.3] months), 719 patients (61.2%) had received 1 regimen, 253 (21.6%) had received 2 regimens, and 202 (17.2%) had received 3 or more regimens. Of the 357 patients harboring druggable driver alterations, 324 (90.8%) had received targeted therapy.

Details of the first-line treatments received by patients with positive results for each driver gene change are shown in eTable 6 in Supplement 1. The proportion of patients who received targeted therapy as first line were 263 of 278 (94.6%) with _EGFR_ variations, 25 of 32 (78.1%) with _ALK_ fusion, 15 of 24 (62.5%) with _ROS1_ fusion, 9 of 12 (75.0%) with the _BRAF_ V600E variation, and 12 of 19 (63.2%) with _MET_ exon 14 skipping. eTable 7 in Supplement 1 shows the patient background of both the groups, the one that received targeted therapy and the one that did not. We observed a trend of more women having received targeted therapy. Nonadenocarcinomas were more common in the group that did not receive targeted therapy. The median overall survival of patients with positive results for the driver gene alteration who received targeted therapy was 24.3 (95% CI, not reported) months; for those with positive findings for the driver gene alteration who did not receive targeted therapy, 15.2 (95% CI, 7.7 to not reported); and for those with negative findings for the driver gene alteration, 11.0 (95% CI, 10.0-12.5) months (_P_< .001) (Figure 3).

## Discussion

To our knowledge, no reports have shown the current status of biomarker testing independently of histological subtype and patient background in Japan. This study revealed the real-world status of biomarker testing in patients with unresectable, advanced, or recurrent NSCLC. Multigene testing in Japan is not sufficiently implemented for nonadenocarcinomas and adenocarcinomas, accounting for 705 (47.7%) of all NSCLC cases.

Use of multigene testing has increased in the US, from 28.3% in 2015 to 68.1% in 2020.13 Contrastingly, in many Asian countries, such as China, Malaysia, and Thailand, multigene testing has not been introduced, and genetic tests other than those for _EGFR_ and _ALK_ are not reimbursed.14,15,16 Asian lung cancer experts have provided consensus recommendations for NSCLC biomarker testing for clinicians working in Asia to improve patient care. These guidelines state that along with programmed cell death 1 ligand 1 (_PDL1_) expression, clinicians should assess for driver alterations in _EGFR_, _ALK_, and _ROS1_ simultaneously, as biomarker testing before initial therapy of metastatic adenocarcinoma and depending on the resources and therapeutic products available, potentially informative or actionable alterations should also be assessed in other genes (_BRAF_ V600E, _RET_, _MET_ exon 14 skipping, _KRAS_, _ERBB2_, and _NTRK_).17

Furthermore, if multiple genes are tested, a panel test should be considered rather than sequential single-gene testing for individual biomarkers. In Japan, several points have been reached through expert consensus. The REVEAL study data showed high _EGFR_, _ALK_, and _ROS1_ testing rates. Tests for other druggable genes, such as _BRAF_ and _RET_, are available. However, approximately half of the cases in the REVEAL study did not undergo multigene testing. This is a key issue in the treatment of lung cancer in Japan. It is necessary that Japan, along with other Asian countries, should promote multigene testing as a common goal.

The proportion of multigene testing was directly reflected in the _BRAF_ and _MET_ testing rates. In Japan, NGS-based tests are used as CDx for targeted agents in _BRAF_ and _MET_ alteration-positive NSCLC. Multigene testing has become increasingly important because some drivers, such as the _RET_ fusion, have recently been approved only for multigene testing as a CDx for targeted therapy. More widely implemented multigene testing is essential for administering targeted therapies to patients with rare genetic drivers. However, the success rate after the initial introduction of the Oncomine DxTT multiple CDx system was insufficient in a recent study.10 Therefore, the quantity and quality of the specimens require optimization. These results possibly occurred because the higher specimen quality and quantity required for this test was compared with that needed for single-gene testing. This is one of the most substantial factors contributing to the lack of widespread use of multigene testing in Japan. It is generally recognized that surgical specimens, for which more specimens are available, are more suitable for genetic testing; however, this was not the case with the REVEAL study. Therefore, further detailed investigations are warranted. The efforts of clinicians to improve the quantity and quality of biopsy specimens have improved success rates. The 2 approved multigene tests that allow for variations in the required quality and quantity of specimens would further benefit clinicians by allowing them to use specimens with varying quality and quantity, depending on the condition of the specimen.

The results of multigene tests can differ from those of single-gene tests, as in the discordant cases in this study. There are 2 main reasons for this finding. First, due to the characteristics of NGS, it tends to be less sensitive than PCR and other tests. Second, the coverage of each test differs for each genetic alteration subtype. In the REVEAL study data, although a small number of cases was analyzed, a trend toward lower positive concordance rates for _ALK_ and _ROS1_ and lower negative concordance rates for _MET_ occurred, because false-positive findings for _MET_ exon 14 skipping have been reported with the Oncomine DxTT, which is not approved as a CDx, and validation with single-gene testing is recommended.18

Similarly, IHC, as single-gene testing for _ROS1,_ has not been approved as a CDx due to the high number of false-positive findings reported (eTable 8 in Supplement 1).19 However, IHC, as single-gene testing for _ALK,_ which has high sensitivity, has been approved as a CDx (eTable 8 in Supplement 1). The quality and quantity of specimens submitted to Oncomine DxTT may have affected the results; however, this is unknown, because such information was not collected in the REVEAL study.

Poor ECOG-PS, SCC, and other comorbidities were background factors associated with not performing multigene testing. _MET_ alterations are frequently detected in nonadenocarcinoma,20 similar to our data. There is concern that _MET_ alterations might be frequently missed by single-gene testing because they are less frequent and tend to be a lower priority for testing. Therefore, multigene testing should be performed more frequently in patients without adenocarcinoma. In addition, some targeted therapies, such as osimertinib mesylate21,22 and alectinib hydrochloride,23 have been safely administered to patients with poor ECOG-PS. In vulnerable patients, treatment options are limited. Therefore, providing opportunities for these patients to undergo multigene testing is important. Furthermore, perioperative treatments for NSCLC positive for driver gene alterations have been developed, and further discussion is needed on when and which genes should be tested.

Approximately 90% of patients harboring any druggable driver alteration in this study received at least 1 targeted therapy. However, when considering each driver gene, driver alterations other than those in _EGFR_ were found to have lower rates of targeted induction as a first-line therapy. Shimizu et al24 showed that first-line treatment with an EGFR–tyrosine kinase inhibitor in the single-gene testing era was administered to 93.3% of patients with positive test results for the biomarker; _ALK_ inhibitor, to 93.3%; and ROS1 inhibitor, to 100%. The discrepancy between the previous report and the REVEAL study results can be attributed to the fact that the study did not strictly assess the status of biomarker testing before the initial treatment and that the results of biomarker testing were only known in some cases after the first-line treatment had been initiated. The prognosis for patients with positive findings for the driver gene alteration without targeted therapy was not different from that for patients with negative findings in the REVEAL study.25 In addition, some patients with positive findings for the driver gene alteration did not receive target therapy. There could be background difficulties in providing targeted therapies; however, we hope that appropriate therapies are provided as much as possible. The prognosis of patients with advanced or recurrent lung cancer could be improved by performing appropriate biomarker testing and initiating the relevant targeted therapies.

### Limitations

This study has several limitations. The data set is not a collection of consecutive cases; therefore, selection bias cannot be eliminated. However, this bias could be minimized by entering a large number of cases (eg, 1500) from numerous facilities. In addition, as stated previously, certain results of biomarker testing were only known after the initiation of first-line treatment. Finally, the study has limited generalizability to a broader population because the investigational sites were institutions that joined the WJOG and requested participation. Most were specialized cancer care institutions. These results may not reflect the approaches to biomarker testing in institutions without specialists.

## Conclusions

The findings of the REVEAL cohort study suggest that multigene testing has not been sufficiently implemented in Japan and should be performed even in nonadenocarcinomas and patients with poor ECOG-PS to avoid missing rare driver gene alterations. Follow-up data, including mature data on treatment and survival, will be analyzed in the REVEAL trial in the future.

## About this book

 Recent advances in electron microscopy have opened up new dimensions and perspectives in the field of morphology, and these are presently being integrated with biochemical and physiopathological phenomena occurring in cells, tissues, and organs. Methods such as freeze-fracture, freeze-etching, scanning, and high-voltage electron microscopy have contributed immensely to this progress, as well as to the study of smooth muscle tissue and contractile cells in general. The articles composing this book have been selected and edited with the purpose of updating and reviewing the most important aspects of smooth muscle cells as revealed by the integration of these submicroscopic techniques. The chapters of this volume have been prepared by some of the most authoritative experts in the discipline. Therefore each article not only offers the reader a concise review of the specific topic, but also seeks to highlight areas that require further investigation. Much of the volume is presented in an illustrative format so as to emphasize the remarkable results obtainable by the combination of the aforementioned methods, which allow a better appreciation of smooth muscle structure and ultrastructure. This volume, like others in the series, is intended not only for researchers in the field, but also for graduate students of histology, embryology, anatomy, physiology, and pathology in both medical and veterinary colleges. My hope is that this book will prove to be a valuable academic resource to the audience of the world in this fascinating and expanding field.

# High school students receive Merit Award at Singapore International Mathematical and Computational Challenge 2.0

[![Image 9: RSS](https://www.titech.ac.jp/common/img/ico-rss01-no.gif)](https://www.titech.ac.jp/english/news/rss.xml)

*   [Prizes](https://www.titech.ac.jp/english/news/prize) 
*   [Students](https://www.titech.ac.jp/english/news/students) 

Published: January 6, 2023

Three students from Tokyo Tech High School of Science and Technology have won the Merit Award in the Senior Challenge category of Singapore International Mathematical and Computational Challenge 2.0 (SIMC2.0) 2022. The contest, held from November 9 to 12, included teams from schools representing 23 countries and regions in the Senior Challenge category.

![Image 10: Merit Award winners (from left): Isozaki, Goto, Suzaki](https://www.titech.ac.jp/english/news/img/news-31468-31578-p1.jpg)

Merit Award winners (from left): Isozaki, Goto, Suzaki

SIMC is an international mathematics contest which has been hosted every alternate year since 2008 by NUS (National University of Singapore) High School of Mathematics and Science in collaboration with Singapore's Ministry of Education. This year's contest included a new programming component, making SIMC 2.0 more suited to the learning needs of students in the current era.

Tokyo Tech High School of Science and Technology has participated in the contest since 2012, making this their fifth appearance.

## Recipients of Merit Award

*    Natsuki Isozaki, 3rd year, Applied Chemistry 
*    Kai Suzaki, 3rd year, Applied Chemistry 
*    Ryoei Goto, 1st year 

### Comments from team leader Natsuki Isozaki

The questions at SIMC have gradually evolved, and this year's competition featured a Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) model applied to infectious diseases. With limited time to work on the problem, the three members of our team worked hard while combining our strengths. The report, presentation, and Q&A session in English were particularly challenging. I am very pleased to have received this award as a representative of Tokyo Tech High School of Science and Technology.

# High school students receive Merit Award at Singapore International Mathematical and Computational Challenge 2.0

[![Image 9: RSS](https://www.titech.ac.jp/common/img/ico-rss01-no.gif)](https://www.titech.ac.jp/english/news/rss.xml)

*   [Prizes](https://www.titech.ac.jp/english/news/prize) 
*   [Students](https://www.titech.ac.jp/english/news/students) 

Published: January 6, 2023

Three students from Tokyo Tech High School of Science and Technology have won the Merit Award in the Senior Challenge category of Singapore International Mathematical and Computational Challenge 2.0 (SIMC2.0) 2022. The contest, held from November 9 to 12, included teams from schools representing 23 countries and regions in the Senior Challenge category.

![Image 10: Merit Award winners (from left): Isozaki, Goto, Suzaki](https://www.titech.ac.jp/english/news/img/news-31468-31578-p1.jpg)

Merit Award winners (from left): Isozaki, Goto, Suzaki

SIMC is an international mathematics contest which has been hosted every alternate year since 2008 by NUS (National University of Singapore) High School of Mathematics and Science in collaboration with Singapore's Ministry of Education. This year's contest included a new programming component, making SIMC 2.0 more suited to the learning needs of students in the current era.

Tokyo Tech High School of Science and Technology has participated in the contest since 2012, making this their fifth appearance.

## Recipients of Merit Award

*    Natsuki Isozaki, 3rd year, Applied Chemistry 
*    Kai Suzaki, 3rd year, Applied Chemistry 
*    Ryoei Goto, 1st year 

### Comments from team leader Natsuki Isozaki

The questions at SIMC have gradually evolved, and this year's competition featured a Susceptible-Infected-Recovered (SIR) model applied to infectious diseases. With limited time to work on the problem, the three members of our team worked hard while combining our strengths. The report, presentation, and Q&A session in English were particularly challenging. I am very pleased to have received this award as a representative of Tokyo Tech High School of Science and Technology.

 French Description Government registration of vital statistics (baptism, marriage and death) did not begin until the late 1800s. For the time period prior to that, records of local churches are the chief source for vital statistics.   
 In this collection can be found parish registers and other church records from various churches in the province of Quebec.   
 There are many points to note when using these registers. For instance, be aware that denominations can change. Lutheran records, for example, may sometimes be found in Anglican registers, while Presbyterian and Methodist records are now frequently found with those of successor congregations belonging to the United Church of Canada. Note also that parish boundaries can change, so that settlements may be served by different parish churches.
